title: IYT VHF Radio Operator
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the IYT VHF Radio Operator syllabus. Not official IYT exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

questions.q: A new crew member asks which control keeps the radio quiet between calls without cutting anyone out. What do you show them?
options: The squelch, set just past the point where the hiss stops
The dual watch button, so it listens less
The power switch, set to low power, 1 W
The volume, turned right down until it is silent
questions.why: Squelch mutes background hiss; set just past the hiss so weak stations still open it.

questions.q: A friend says he called you twice this afternoon, but you heard nothing. What is the most likely reason?

figure.title: Your VHF since lunch
lines: Not a sound for three hours

options: Half volume mutes stations more than 5 miles away
The squelch is so high that weaker signals cannot open it
The 25 W setting drowns out stations that call you
Channel 16 stays silent unless DSC is switched on
questions.why: Squelch turned right up cuts out everything but strong signals; back it off to just past the hiss.

questions.q: Your friend's yacht does not answer. What do you change first?

figure.title: Calling a friend
lines: Her yacht: 12 miles away, open water

options: Switch to dual watch and call again on 1 W
Stay on 1 W and call again straight away
Switch to high power, 25 W, and call again
Turn the squelch up and call again on 1 W
questions.why: Low power, 1 W, is for short range; at 12 miles you need 25 W.

questions.q: You expect calls from the marina on its working channel and from your friend on 72, and you must keep listening to 16. Which function do you use?
options: Dual watch on 16 and channel 72 only
Low power with the squelch turned fully up
Channel 70 set to receive voice calls
Tri-watch: 16 plus the two channels you choose
questions.why: Tri-watch checks 16 and two other channels in turn; dual watch covers only one besides 16.

questions.q: The marina says your calls arrive as "…is Aurora, OVER" — the start is always missing. What are you doing wrong?
options: Speaking the instant you press; pause a moment, then speak
Holding the microphone a hand's width from your mouth
Calling with the squelch set too low on your own set
Transmitting on 25 W instead of 1 W so close by
questions.why: The set needs a moment after you press the button; words spoken at once are clipped.

questions.q: Your crew calls the marina, shouting with the microphone pressed to his lips. The marina cannot understand him. What do you tell him?
options: Keep it at his lips but switch to high power, 25 W
Hold it a few centimetres away and speak in a normal voice
Keep it at his lips and turn the squelch down
Hold it at arm's length and shout a little louder
questions.why: Shouting into a mic held at the lips distorts speech; a few centimetres and a normal voice is clearest.

questions.q: The marina complains that someone has blocked its working channel for ten minutes. Then you notice the scene in the figure. What is happening?

figure.title: In the cockpit
lines: Jammed in a locker under fenders
You hear nothing from the marina

options: Low power on the fixed set leaks onto other channels
The fixed set is relaying 16 onto the marina channel
The handheld's transmit button is pressed in the locker
The handheld's low battery makes it send a carrier
questions.why: A jammed press-to-talk button transmits non-stop and blocks the channel for everyone.

questions.q: Your charter yacht has its VHF antenna on the pushpit rail, not at the masthead. What do you expect compared with a masthead antenna?
options: Better range on 16 but shorter on working channels
The same range, as height does not matter on VHF
Longer range, because the cable to the set is shorter
Shorter range, because the antenna is much lower
questions.why: VHF range depends mainly on antenna height; a low antenna sees a closer horizon.

questions.q: Your radio checks now reach only a mile or two. What do you do?

figure.title: After the winter
lines: Antenna cable joint at the mast foot

options: Clean or replace the connector before relying on the set
Use channel 70 by voice, as it carries further
Turn the squelch to minimum to hear stations better
Switch to low power to protect the set from damage
questions.why: A corroded antenna connection loses most of the signal; fix the coax and connectors.

questions.q: You call the coast station and it reports your signal as weak. What do you do first?

lines: Engine off since yesterday, fridge running

options: Switch to channel 70 and repeat the call by voice
Run the engine to charge the battery, then call again
Turn your own squelch up and call again at once
Lower the antenna, as you are too close to the station
questions.why: A fixed set needs a healthy supply; at low voltage it cannot transmit at full power.

questions.q: You are 20 miles offshore and need to reach the coast station. You have the fixed set with a masthead antenna and a handheld. Which do you use?
options: The handheld: it is closer to your mouth and clearer
The handheld, held up as high as you can in the cockpit
The fixed set: more power and a much higher antenna
Either: both reach the same distance on channel 16
questions.why: A masthead antenna and 25 W reach far beyond a handheld's few miles.

questions.q: You are going ashore in the dinghy for the afternoon. The handheld shows one bar of battery. What do you do?
options: Leave it aboard and rely on someone's mobile phone
Take it on scan mode, which uses less battery
Take it as it is — one bar lasts a whole afternoon
Charge it or fit a charged battery pack before you leave
questions.why: Transmitting drains a handheld fast; one bar may die when you press the button.

questions.q: Your handheld is marked IPX7. What may you rely on?
options: It survives a short dunking, about 1 m for 30 minutes
It floats if it is dropped over the side
It needs no fresh-water rinse after spray
It can be used under water to about 10 m
questions.why: IPX7 means protected against brief immersion; it does not mean it floats.

questions.q: The marina is about 6 miles away over open water. How do you give the handheld its best chance?

figure.title: Handheld only
lines: Called from the cockpit: no reply

options: Go below to the chart table, out of the wind
Stand up on deck, high power, antenna straight up
Hold it flat with the antenna aimed at the marina
Stay in the cockpit and switch to low power
questions.why: Range comes from height and a vertical antenna; cabin and cockpit coamings block the signal.

questions.q: You want to check that the radio on your new charter yacht works. How do you do it?
options: Make a short voice call on channel 70 to all ships
Call "radio check, all stations" on 16 at low power
Ask the marina or another boat for a check on a working channel
Call "radio check, all stations" on 16 at high power
questions.why: Radio checks go on a working channel, never on 16 or 70.

questions.q: You switch on the fixed VHF before leaving and the display stays blank. What do you check first?
options: The antenna cable connector at the top of the mast
The squelch, in case it is turned fully up
The DSC settings, in case the MMSI is missing
The VHF breaker on the switch panel and the battery switch
questions.why: No display means no power: check the breaker, fuse and battery switch before anything else.

questions.q: The antenna cable is unplugged from the set while you fix the connector. Your crew wants to press the button "just to test it". What do you say?
options: No — transmitting without an antenna can damage the set
Fine — it simply transmits a shorter range
Fine, as long as it is on channel 16
Fine on low power, 1 W, for a few seconds
questions.why: With no antenna the power has nowhere to go and can damage the transmitter.

questions.q: You are about to abandon ship into the liferaft. The fixed VHF and a charged waterproof handheld are aboard. Which radio goes with you?
options: The fixed set, unplugged and wrapped in a bin bag
The waterproof handheld, kept in the grab bag or on you
The fixed set's handset, unplugged from the set
Neither: the liferaft has its own radio built in
questions.why: Only a handheld works away from the boat's antenna and batteries.

questions.q: You call the marina from the helm in a strong wind. They hear mostly a roar. What do you do?
options: Turn the squelch down so your voice opens it
Switch to high power so the voice cuts through
Shield the microphone from the wind and speak normally
Shout louder with the microphone held further away
questions.why: Wind across the microphone drowns speech; shelter it with your hand or body.

questions.q: Which pair can usually talk over the longest distance?
options: Two handhelds, each held up in a cockpit
A handheld in a cockpit and a masthead set
Two yachts, each with a masthead antenna
A yacht's masthead set and a coast station on a hill
questions.why: Range grows with the height of both antennas; a hilltop coast station sees furthest.

questions.q: You are under way along the coast and not talking to anyone. Which channel do you keep the radio on?
options: Channel 16, the distress, safety and calling channel
Channel 70, so you hear the coastguard by voice
Channel 13, the channel used by all leisure craft
Channel 6, the intership channel for yachts
questions.why: Under way, keep watch on 16 so you hear distress and safety calls and anyone calling you.

questions.q: Your crew scrolls to channel 70 to call a friend, but the set will not let him talk there. Why?
options: Channel 70 is for marinas and needs their permission
Channel 70 carries only DSC digital calls, never voice
Channel 70 is kept for the coastguard's voice traffic
Channel 70 only works for voice on high power, 25 W
questions.why: Channel 70 is reserved for DSC data; voice there would block distress alerts.

questions.q: A ship crossing ahead calls you on 16 and asks you to go to channel 13. What is 13 for?

figure.note: The ship calls you on 16: "go to 13"

options: DSC alerts and calls between ships
Public calls to telephones ashore
Bridge-to-bridge navigation safety between vessels
Port operations inside the harbour
questions.why: Channel 13 is the international bridge-to-bridge channel for navigation safety.

questions.q: You want to call a yacht you met yesterday. You do not know which channel they listen to. Where do you make the first call?
options: On the nearest marina's channel
On 13, then stay there to talk
On 70, then move to a working channel
On 16, then move to a working channel
questions.why: 16 is the calling channel; once in contact, both move off it.

questions.q: Your friend answers your call on 16. Which channel do you suggest for the conversation?
options: An intership channel such as 72 or 77
Channel 70, because it is always quiet
Stay on 16, as the chat will be short
The marina's port operations channel
questions.why: Yacht-to-yacht talk goes on an intership simplex channel, not 16, 70 or a port channel.

questions.q: You and a friend want a long chat about tomorrow's route. Both 6 and 72 are free. Which do you choose?
options: 6 — it is the intership channel meant for chats
72 — keep 6 clear, as it is also used in search and rescue
72 — channel 6 is only for DSC data and alerts
6 — it carries further than 72 at the same power
questions.why: Channel 6 is also the on-scene channel for search and rescue; use 72 or 77 for social talk.

questions.q: You and your friend both select the same duplex channel. You can hear the coast station on it, but not each other. Why?
options: Duplex channels are receive-only for small craft
Duplex channels need both sets on high power
Each yacht sends on one frequency and listens on another
Your squelch is set too high for a duplex channel
questions.why: On duplex a ship sends on one frequency and receives the shore's; two ships cannot hear each other.

questions.q: The coast station asks you to switch to its working channel, which is duplex. Can you talk to it there?
options: No — duplex works only between two ships
No — yachts may only use simplex channels
Only if you first send a DSC call on 70
Yes — duplex works between a ship and a shore station
questions.why: Duplex channels are made for ship-to-shore calls; only ship-to-ship fails on them.

questions.q: On channel 72 you and your friend press the transmit button at the same moment. What happens?
options: Neither hears the other — on simplex only one can transmit at a time
The set holds the second call until the first ends
Both are heard, as in a telephone conversation
The stronger signal is passed on to the other boat
questions.why: Simplex is one frequency: while you transmit you cannot receive, so talk in turn and end with OVER.

questions.q: You are approaching an island port in Greece and want the port authority's working channel. Where do you find it?
options: It is always channel 70, as for all port calls
In the pilot book, almanac or port details on the chart
Ask any yacht on 72 which channel they think it is
It is always channel 12 in every Greek port
questions.why: Port channels differ from port to port; look them up rather than guess.

questions.q: Your friend cannot hear you, although you are only 6 miles apart. Why?

figure.note: A: you · B: your friend, 6 miles away

options: The island's harbour channel jams the intership one
Six miles is beyond the range of any yacht VHF
VHF works roughly in line of sight, and the island is in the way
VHF bends around islands only on channel 16
questions.why: VHF travels roughly in straight lines; high land between the antennas blocks it.

questions.q: Which of these may stay on channel 16 instead of moving to another channel?
options: A friendly chat between two yachts
Booking a berth with the marina
The coastguard's full weather forecast
Distress traffic: a MAYDAY and the replies to it
questions.why: 16 is for distress, urgency, safety and calling; only distress traffic normally stays on it.

questions.q: You are approaching a busy commercial port where large ships manoeuvre. Which channel do you listen to as well as 16?
options: The port's own operations or traffic channel
No other channel — 16 is enough in a port
Channel 70, to hear the ships' DSC alerts
Channel 72, where ships give way to yachts
questions.why: Near a busy port, listen on its listed port or traffic channel to know what ships will do.

questions.q: On your charter yacht in Croatia, the VHF display shows "USA" next to the channel number. What do you do?
options: Set the mode to CAN, as used in Europe
Set the channel mode to international (INT)
Leave it: channel modes only matter for DSC
Leave it: USA mode gives the longest range
questions.why: Outside North America use the international channel plan; some channels differ in USA mode.

questions.q: You and your friend move to 72, but two other boats are already talking there. What do you do?
options: Use channel 70, which is always free
Go back to 16 and have your chat there
Agree another free intership channel, such as 77
Talk over them — 72 is open to everyone
questions.why: Never talk over others; pick another free intership channel.

questions.q: Your flotilla agreed this morning to keep a watch on 72 as well as 16. You want to reach the lead boat. Where do you call?
options: On 16 first, then move to 72
On 70, then talk on 72
On 6, then move to 72
Directly on 72, as agreed beforehand
questions.why: A pre-arranged working channel can be used for the call itself, keeping 16 clear.

questions.q: Which set of channels fits these three jobs, in order?

figure.title: Three jobs
lines: 1. Agree how to pass a ship that called you
2. A long chat with a friend's yacht
3. The channel your DSC uses for alerts

questions.why: 13 bridge-to-bridge safety, 72 intership chat, 70 DSC only.

questions.q: From A you talk easily to the coast station, but your friends at B cannot hear you. Why?

labels: coast station on a mountain, 30 miles north
figure.note: A: you · B: your friends, 3 miles away

options: The coast station is on duplex, which carries further
The coast station's antenna is very high; the headland blocks B
Friends' sets need DSC to hear a yacht nearby
Short distances are weaker than long ones on VHF
questions.why: Range depends on antenna height and a clear line; high stations reach far, land in between blocks.

questions.q: Channel 16 is busy with a long MAYDAY exchange between the coastguard and a yacht. You need to tell the marina you will be late. What do you do?
options: Wait for a gap and call the marina on 16
Call the marina briefly on 16 at low power
Call the marina directly on its working channel
Call the marina on 70, which stays free
questions.why: Keep off 16 during distress traffic; routine calls go straight to the working channel.

questions.q: Your three flotilla friends are at sea in these places. Both your boats have masthead antennas. Whom can you count on reaching by voice?

figure.title: Where they are
lines: A: 8 miles away, open water between
B: 12 miles, behind a 400 m island
C: 40 miles away, open water between

options: A and B
A and C
All three
A only
questions.why: Yacht to yacht reaches roughly 10–20 miles over open water; high land between blocks it.

questions.q: You want to call the yacht Blue Star. Which call is correctly built?
options: "Blue Star, Blue Star, Blue Star, this is Aurora, Aurora, Aurora, OVER"
"Aurora, Aurora, Aurora, calling Blue Star, Blue Star, OVER"
"Hello Blue Star, it's Aurora here, do you read me? Over"
"Blue Star, this is Aurora, please answer, OVER AND OUT"
questions.why: The station called first (up to three times), then THIS IS and your own name, then OVER.

questions.q: You have finished talking to the marina and need no reply. How do you end your last transmission?
options: OVER, STANDING BY
OUT
OVER
OVER AND OUT
questions.why: OVER asks for a reply, OUT ends the exchange; the two never go together.

questions.q: You switch to 72 to call a friend and hear two other boats in the middle of a conversation. What do you do?
options: Call your friend on 16 and stay there to talk
Make your call at once — 72 is open to all
Wait until they finish, then make your call
Break in with BREAK, BREAK and then call
questions.why: Always listen before you transmit and never talk over a conversation in progress.

questions.q: From your berth you want to call the fuel dock, 200 m across the marina. The set is on 25 W. What do you do first?
options: Leave it on 25 W, but keep the call very short
Switch to dual watch so you hear their reply
Leave it on 25 W, so they hear you clearly
Switch to low power, 1 W — it is plenty at this range
questions.why: In port use 1 W: it reaches the dock without blocking the channel for boats further away.

questions.q: On 16 you hear: "Aurora, this is Blue Star, OVER" in reply to your call. What do you say next?
options: "Blue Star, this is Aurora, channel seven two, OVER"
"Blue Star, this is Aurora, we are anchoring tonight in…"
Nothing — just switch to 72 and wait for them there
"Blue Star, this is Aurora, channel seven zero, OVER"
questions.why: Once contact is made on 16, propose an intership working channel and move there to talk.

questions.q: Blue Star has agreed to move to 72. You switch over. What do you do there?
options: Start your message at once without calling them
Listen a moment, then call: "Blue Star, this is Aurora, OVER"
Wait in silence until Blue Star calls you first
Call "All stations, this is Aurora" so they find you
questions.why: On the new channel, check it is free, then call the station again before your message.

questions.q: You want a berth for tonight. How do you make the first call?

figure.title: Arriving at Vega Marina
lines: Pilot book lists the marina's VHF channel
You are 1 mile off the entrance

options: On 72: "Any marina staff, this is Aurora, OVER"
On 16, giving your whole request in one transmission
On the marina's channel: "Vega Marina, this is Aurora, OVER"
On 70 by voice, as marinas keep watch on it
questions.why: Call a marina on its own working channel with a short call; the request follows once it answers.

questions.q: You call the marina on its working channel and get no answer. What do you do?
options: Call again straight away, a little louder
Call them by voice on 70 to get attention
Keep calling every 15 seconds until they answer
Wait a few minutes before you call again
questions.why: Leave a gap of a few minutes between calls; non-stop calling blocks the channel.

questions.q: The marina answers your call. What do you say?

figure.title: Marina channel, a busy evening
lines: Marina: "Aurora, this is Vega Marina, OVER"

options: Your request in one short message: boat, length, nights
The whole story first, so they see why you need it
Your request on 16 instead, so others hear it too
Nothing yet — wait for them to ask each detail
questions.why: Keep calls short and to the point so others can use the channel.

questions.q: The marina asks you to pay in advance for the berth. Your crew starts to read the credit card number over the radio. What do you do?
options: Let him, but on a duplex channel, which is private
Stop him — anyone listening can hear it; pay in the office
Let him, as long as he spells it phonetically
Let him, but switch to low power, 1 W, first
questions.why: VHF is open to everyone in range; never give card numbers or other private data on air.

questions.q: You hear: "Aurora, Aurora, this is Blue Star, OVER". How do you answer?
options: "Aurora here, go ahead, OVER AND OUT"
"Blue Star, Blue Star, Aurora receiving"
"Blue Star, this is Aurora, OVER"
"This is Aurora, Aurora, Aurora, OUT"
questions.why: Answer with the caller's name, THIS IS, your name and OVER.

questions.q: You have just asked the marina whether they have a berth for a 12 m yacht. How do you end this transmission?
options: Just release the button and say nothing
OUT — the marina will answer when ready
OVER AND OUT — to be extra clear
OVER — you are waiting for their answer
questions.why: End every transmission that needs a reply with OVER so the other station knows to speak.

questions.q: You proposed 72 to Blue Star. They reply: "Aurora, this is Blue Star, seven seven, OVER". What do you do?
options: Reply "seven seven", switch to 77 and call them there
Insist on 72, since you proposed it first
Go to 72 anyway and wait for them there
Stay on 16 and talk there until you agree
questions.why: The called station may propose another channel; agree it briefly and move.

questions.q: At anchor, the children ask to play with the handheld and call each other on 16. What do you say?
options: Yes, but on channel 70 rather than 16
No — 16 must be kept clear and the radio is not a toy
Yes, as long as the handheld is on low power
Yes, as long as each call is kept short
questions.why: Channel 16 must stay free for distress and calling; needless transmissions are not allowed.

questions.q: The marina ends with: "…we will meet you at the fuel dock, OUT". What do you do?
options: Reply "Vega Marina, this is Aurora, OUT"
Reply "OVER AND OUT" to close it properly
Nothing more — the exchange is over; go back to watching 16
Reply "Received, OVER" and wait for an answer
questions.why: OUT means the exchange is finished; no reply is expected.

questions.q: Entering harbour, you hear: "Yacht entering harbour, this is Port Authority, state your name and intentions, OVER". How do you answer?
options: "All stations, this is Aurora, mooring at the quay, OUT"
"Received, Aurora entering harbour, OVER AND OUT"
"Port Authority, this is Aurora, standing by, OUT"
"Port Authority, this is Aurora, mooring at the town quay, OVER"
questions.why: Answer the station that called you, give what it asked for and end with OVER.

questions.q: Which line of this exchange breaks radio procedure?

figure.title: Your call to the marina
lines: 1 You: Vega Marina ×3, this is Aurora, OVER
2 Marina: Aurora, this is Vega Marina, OVER
3 You: a berth for one night, 12 m, OVER
4 You: thanks, see you soon, OVER AND OUT

options: Line 4
Line 1
Line 3
Line 2
questions.why: OVER asks for a reply and OUT ends the exchange; "OVER AND OUT" contradicts itself.

questions.q: What is the sensible next step?

figure.title: Calling ahead for a berth
lines: Marina 18 miles ahead, behind a cape
Two calls 10 minutes apart: no reply
Power 25 W, radio check fine this morning

options: Send a PAN-PAN so the marina takes notice
Try again later, when you are closer to the marina
Ask all stations on 16 to pass your request on
Keep calling every minute until someone answers
questions.why: No reply at long range usually means out of range or busy; call again nearer, not more often.

questions.q: In a crowded bay a motor yacht is dropping its anchor across your chain. You do not know its name. How do you call it?
options: "All stations, all stations, this is Aurora, a boat is on my chain, OVER"
"PAN-PAN ×3, motor yacht in Vathi Bay, you are over my chain, OVER"
"Motor yacht anchoring north of me in Vathi Bay, this is Aurora, OVER"
"Hello, the boat anchoring now, are you there? Aurora, OVER AND OUT"
questions.why: If you do not know a vessel's name, identify it by type and position instead.

questions.q: Blue Star agreed on 16 to move to 72. On 72 you call them twice, a minute apart, with no reply. What do you do?
options: Wait on 72 in silence for an hour
Call them by voice on 70 instead
Keep calling on 72 every few seconds
Go back to 16 and call them once more
questions.why: If the other station does not appear on the working channel, return to where you last had contact.

questions.q: The marina asks you to spell your yacht's name, KIRA. What do you say?
options: "Kilo India Romeo Alfa"
"King Item Roger Able"
"Kilo India Roger Apple"
"Kilo Italy Romeo Alfa"
questions.why: The phonetic alphabet: K Kilo, I India, R Romeo, A Alfa.

questions.q: The marina's reply is drowned out by an engine starting nearby; you understood nothing. What do you send?
options: WAIT
SAY AGAIN
CORRECTION
REPEAT
questions.why: SAY AGAIN asks for the whole message again; REPEAT is not used for this on the radio.

questions.q: The marina gives you your berth and the code for the shower block. You have understood it all. Which word confirms that?
options: CORRECTION
AFFIRMATIVE
RECEIVED
I SPELL
questions.why: RECEIVED means the message has been heard and understood.

questions.q: You confirm to the marina that your berth is number 9. How do you say the figure?
options: "Nina"
"November"
"Nine-zero"
"Niner"
questions.why: On the radio the figure 9 is spoken "niner" so it is not confused with other words.

questions.q: The marina asks your draft. It is 2.9 m. What do you say?
options: "Two decimal niner metres"
"Twenty-nine metres"
"Two and nine metres"
"Two niner metres"
questions.why: Figures are spoken one by one, with "decimal" for the point and "niner" for 9.

questions.q: You hear: "Aurora, this is Vega Marina, go to pontoon Charlie…" and the rest is lost in noise. What do you send?
options: "SAY AGAIN WORD AFTER Charlie"
"SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER Charlie"
"SAY AGAIN ALL BEFORE Charlie"
"I SPELL Charlie"
questions.why: ALL AFTER asks for everything that followed the word you name.

questions.q: You told the marina: "Berth for one night, catamaran, twelve metres, OVER". They reply: "Aurora, SAY AGAIN ALL BEFORE twelve metres, OVER". What do you repeat?
options: Only the words "twelve metres"
Everything after "twelve metres"
The words before "twelve metres"
Your yacht's name, spelled out
questions.why: ALL BEFORE asks for everything that came before the word named.

questions.q: The marina cannot catch your yacht's name, Xenia. How do you give it?
options: "Xenia, CORRECTION, X-ray Echo November India Alfa"
"Xenia, SAY AGAIN, X-ray Echo November India Alfa"
"Xenia, I SPELL, Xylophone Echo Nancy India Alfa"
"Xenia, I SPELL, X-ray Echo November India Alfa"
questions.why: I SPELL tells the listener the next words are letters of the phonetic alphabet.

questions.q: You have just said "length one four metres", but Aurora is 12 m long. What do you say at once?
options: "CORRECTION, length one two metres"
"I SPELL, length one two metres"
"WAIT, length one two metres"
"SAY AGAIN, length one two metres"
questions.why: CORRECTION cancels your last word or phrase; the right version follows.

questions.q: The marina asks for your boat's registration number. It is in the papers below and will take you a couple of minutes to find. Which proword do you use first?
options: SAY AGAIN
WAIT
AFFIRMATIVE
STATION CALLING
questions.why: WAIT, with the minutes if you can, tells the other station you need a pause.

questions.q: The marina asks: "Aurora, do you need shore power, OVER?" You do. What do you reply?
options: "CORRECTION, OVER"
"RECEIVED, OVER"
"AFFIRMATIVE, OVER"
"I SPELL, OVER"
questions.why: AFFIRMATIVE means yes; RECEIVED only says you heard the question.

questions.q: You hear "Aurora, Aurora, this is …" but the caller's name is lost in noise. How do you answer?
options: "All stations, this is Aurora, SAY AGAIN, OVER"
"Who is calling Aurora? Identify yourself, OVER"
"Aurora, this is Aurora, SAY AGAIN, OUT"
"Station calling Aurora, this is Aurora, OVER"
questions.why: STATION CALLING answers a call when you did not catch who made it.

questions.q: You must read out your latitude. How do you say it?
options: "Three seven degrees five two decimal four minutes north"
"Five two decimal four minutes, three seven degrees north"
"Thirty-seven degrees fifty-two point four minutes north"
"Three seven degrees fifty-two decimal four minutes north"
questions.why: Positions are read figure by figure: degrees, minutes with "decimal", then north or south.

questions.q: The coastguard asks for your MMSI, 237012340. How do you say it?
options: "Two hundred thirty-seven, twelve, three-forty"
"Two three seven zero one two three four zero"
"Twenty-three, seventy, one two, thirty-four, zero"
"Two three seven one two three four"
questions.why: Long numbers are given figure by figure, zeros included.

questions.q: The marina said your berth was "fifteen", and you went to berth 50. How should numbers be given to avoid this?
options: Spelled out: "Foxtrot India Foxtrot…"
As a word, said twice: "fifteen, fifteen"
Figure by figure: "one five"
As a word, said slowly: "fif-teen"
questions.why: Saying figures one by one stops "fifteen" and "fifty" being confused.

questions.q: Your crew calls: "Vega Marina, Aurora, OVER". The marina is unsure who is calling whom. What is missing?
options: I SPELL, before the name of your yacht
OVER AND OUT, at the very end of the call
RECEIVED, before the name of the marina
THIS IS, between the name called and your own name
questions.why: THIS IS separates the station called from the station calling.

questions.q: The marina's reply reaches you like this. What do you send?
options: "SAY AGAIN WORD AFTER pontoon, OVER"
"CORRECTION pontoon, OVER"
"SAY AGAIN WORD BEFORE pontoon, OVER"
"SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER berth, OVER"
questions.why: WORD AFTER asks for the single word that followed the one you name.

questions.q: The coastguard asks your position. How do you read it out?
options: "Thirty-six degrees twenty-seven decimal nine north, twenty-five degrees eight decimal three east"
"Three six degrees two seven decimal niner minutes north, zero two five degrees zero eight decimal three minutes east"
"Three six degrees two seven decimal niner minutes north, two five degrees eight decimal three minutes east"
"Three six degrees two seven decimal niner minutes east, zero two five degrees zero eight decimal three minutes north"
questions.why: Latitude first, then longitude with three figures of degrees; all figures one by one.

questions.q: The marina gives you pontoon B, berth 19. You read it back to confirm. Which is right?
options: "Pontoon Beta, berth one niner"
"Pontoon Bravo, berth nineteen"
"Pontoon Bravo, berth one niner"
"Pontoon Baker, berth one niner"
questions.why: Letters in the phonetic alphabet (B = Bravo), figures one by one with "niner".

questions.q: The marina says: "Aurora, berth one five, CORRECTION, berth one six, pontoon Charlie, OVER". Where do you go?
options: Pontoon C, berth 15 or 16
Pontoon C, berth 15
Pontoon C, berth 56
Pontoon C, berth 16
questions.why: CORRECTION cancels what came just before it; the version after it stands.

questions.q: What do the first three figures of this MMSI, 237, tell a rescue centre?
options: The country where the yacht is registered
The year the radio was installed
The type and size of the vessel
The sea area the yacht is sailing in
questions.why: The first three figures are the MID, the country code of the ship's flag.

questions.q: You are looking through your DSC directory. Which of these numbers belongs to a coast station?
questions.why: A coast station MMSI starts with 00; a group MMSI with a single 0; a ship's with its MID.

questions.q: You buy a DSC handheld and the shop asks for the MMSI to programme it. How many figures will it have?
options: Eleven
Six
Nine
Seven
questions.why: Every MMSI has nine figures.

questions.q: Your DSC set has no GPS connected and no position has been entered. If you send a distress alert, what will be missing?
options: Your MMSI
Your flag country
The word distress
Your position
questions.why: Without a GPS feed or a manual position, the alert says who you are but not where.

questions.q: A guest on your charter yacht wants to put "his own MMSI" into the radio for the week. What do you tell him?
options: No — the MMSI belongs to the yacht and its radio licence
Yes, but only for the length of the charter
Yes, if he also changes the yacht's call sign
Yes — the MMSI belongs to whoever is skipper aboard
questions.why: An MMSI is issued to the vessel with its ship radio licence, not to a person.

questions.q: You know your friend's MMSI and want to call her yacht by DSC for a chat. What do you do?
options: All-ships call proposing 72, then talk on 72
Individual call to her MMSI, proposing 72; talk on 72
Individual call to her MMSI, then talk on 70
Group call to her MMSI, then talk on 16
questions.why: A routine individual call goes to one MMSI and proposes an intership channel for the voice part.

questions.q: Your friend's set acknowledges your DSC call, which proposed channel 72. What happens next?
options: You carry on the chat as DSC text on 70
You must now call her again by voice on 16
Both sets go to 72 and you talk by voice
Both sets go to 16 and you talk there
questions.why: After the acknowledgement both sets switch to the proposed channel for the voice call.

questions.q: Your set rings and shows this. What do you do?
options: Ignore it — group calls are only used for tests
Call the lead on 16 to ask what it is about
Reply to the lead by voice on channel 70
Go to 72 (the set may switch itself) and listen for the lead
questions.why: A group call reaches every set with that group MMSI and sends them all to the proposed channel.

questions.q: You want to ask the boats around you whether anyone has a spare impeller. Should you send an all-ships DSC call?
options: No — all-ships DSC calls are kept for emergencies and safety
Yes, if you propose channel 16 for the replies
Yes, as long as you select low power first
Yes — an all-ships routine call is the right tool
questions.why: All-ships DSC calls are for distress, urgency and safety; routine calls go to one MMSI or a group.

questions.q: Before leaving harbour you see this on the DSC set. What do you do?

figure.title: DSC display
lines: Plotter switched off at the breaker

options: Move the DSC watch from channel 70 to 16
Switch on the GPS feed, or enter the position by hand
Nothing — the MMSI tells rescuers where you are
Test the link by pressing the distress button
questions.why: A distress alert carries your position only if the set has a GPS feed or an up-to-date manual entry.

questions.q: You have decided to send a DSC distress alert. How do you work the red button?
options: Hold it down while you speak the MAYDAY
Press it three times quickly in a row
Lift the cover, then press and hold it for about 5 seconds
Press it once briefly, like a doorbell
questions.why: The distress button sits under a cover and must be held for a few seconds, which prevents accidents.

questions.q: You are about to send a DSC distress alert and have a minute to spare. How do you use it on the set?

figure.title: Holed below the waterline
lines: Water coming in faster than the pumps
About a minute before you must act

options: Enter the coastguard's MMSI, then send
Select "All ships, routine", then send
Choose an intership channel, then send
Select "Flooding" as the nature of distress, then send
questions.why: If there is time, choose the nature of distress from the menu so rescuers know what to bring.

questions.q: No acknowledgement has arrived yet. What is the set doing, and where should you be listening?
options: It repeats the alert by itself; you stay on 16
It has stopped DSC; you call for help on 72
It has given up; you resend the alert by hand
It waits on 70; you speak your MAYDAY there
questions.why: A DSC set repeats a distress alert every few minutes until acknowledged, and sits on 16 for voice.

questions.q: You are deep in a chat on 72 with dual watch switched off. Will your fixed DSC set still receive a distress alert?
options: No — only if dual watch includes channel 70
Yes — it keeps a separate watch on channel 70
No — DSC only works while the set is on 16
Only if the alert comes from a coast station
questions.why: A fixed DSC set has its own receiver that listens on 70 whatever voice channel you use.

questions.q: You want to check that your DSC works before a passage. How do you test it?
options: Send a distress alert, then cancel it at once
Make an all-ships call proposing channel 72
Send an individual call to a friend's MMSI and see it arrive
Call your friend by voice on channel 70
questions.why: Test DSC with a routine individual call; never test with the distress button.

questions.q: There is no time to choose anything from the menu: you lift the cover and hold the button. What does the alert carry?
options: Only your position, without your MMSI
A routine call to the nearest coast station
Nothing — it will not go without a nature chosen
An undesignated distress, with your MMSI and position
questions.why: Sent straight from the button, the alert goes as undesignated distress with your MMSI and position.

questions.q: What do you do now?

figure.title: False alert
lines: A child pressed the red button

options: Cancel it on the set if it can, then tell all stations on 16
Wait for the coastguard to call you first
Switch the radio off and say nothing more
Send a second alert to cancel the first
questions.why: Cancel a false alert by DSC where the set allows, then by voice to all stations on 16.

questions.q: Your DSC set sent a false distress alert at 1420 UTC. Which voice message do you send on 16?
options: "PAN-PAN ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, our alert of 1420 UTC was a mistake"
"All stations ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, cancel my distress alert of 1420 UTC"
"SÉCURITÉ ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, disregard our alert of 1420 UTC"
"MAYDAY ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, our MAYDAY of 1420 UTC is cancelled"
questions.why: A false alert is cancelled to ALL STATIONS with your name, MMSI, position and the time of the alert.

questions.q: Your set sounds an alarm and shows this. What do you do first?
options: Call the yacht by voice on channel 70
Acknowledge the alert by DSC straight away
Silence the alarm, note the details, listen on 16
Relay the alert by DSC to all ships at once
questions.why: Note the alert and listen on 16; acknowledging a DSC distress alert is normally left to the coast station.

questions.q: What does this mean, and what do you do?

figure.title: Check-out at the charter base
lines: You sail for a week tomorrow

options: Use the flotilla's group MMSI as your own for the week
Alerts still go, just without a name; sail as planned
Enter any nine figures yourself so the button works
No DSC call or alert can go out; have the base fix it before you sail
questions.why: Without the yacht's MMSI a DSC set cannot send calls or alerts; the base must programme it.

questions.q: Does this situation justify a MAYDAY?
options: Yes — grave and imminent danger to boat and crew
No — first ask the coastguard if it qualifies
Only if another vessel is in sight to help
No — not until the crew has to abandon ship
questions.why: MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger needing immediate help — an uncontrolled fire is exactly that.

questions.q: Your yacht Blue Dolphin is sinking and you pick up the microphone on channel 16. How does your distress call begin?
options: MAYDAY once, THIS IS, Blue Dolphin once
MAYDAY ×3, THIS IS, Blue Dolphin ×3
THIS IS, Blue Dolphin ×3, then MAYDAY ×3
ALL STATIONS ×3, THIS IS, Blue Dolphin ×3
questions.why: Distress call: MAYDAY three times, THIS IS, the boat's name three times (with call sign or MMSI).

questions.q: You have said MAYDAY three times and THIS IS Blue Dolphin three times, with your call sign. What do you say next?
options: Number of people aboard, then position
OVER, and wait for a reply first
MAYDAY, Blue Dolphin, then your position
Your problem first, then your position
questions.why: The message opens with MAYDAY and the name once more; position comes first — rescuers need it most.

questions.q: In which order do you give these four items in your message?

figure.title: Your MAYDAY message
lines: Help: need pumps and a tow

options: Persons, position, distress, help
Position, persons, help, distress
Distress, help, position, persons
Position, distress, help, persons
questions.why: Order: position, nature of distress, assistance required, persons on board, then other useful information.

questions.q: Your plotter has died and you will give your position relative to something on the chart. Which reference do you choose?
options: A charted lighthouse or headland nearby
The nearest anchored yacht you can see
The marina you left this morning
The name of the beach taverna ashore
questions.why: Bearing and distance must be from a charted point that rescuers can find on their own chart.

questions.q: You read this off the plotter for your MAYDAY. How do you say the position on air?
options: Rounded to whole degrees: 38 N 24 E
Latitude first, then longitude, N and E
Latitude only — that is enough at sea
Longitude first, then latitude, E and N
questions.why: Position by coordinates: latitude first, then longitude, each with N/S or E/W.

questions.q: Is a MAYDAY the right call?
options: Yes — if you cannot reach port by dark
Yes — any engine failure at sea is distress
No — there is no grave and imminent danger
Yes — but sent on low power only
questions.why: No grave and imminent danger, no MAYDAY: sail on, or ask for help with a lower-priority call.

questions.q: You have sent your MAYDAY on 16 and, after listening for a while, nobody answers. What do you do?
options: Stop transmitting to save the battery
Wait a full hour before calling again
Move to channel 6 and call only there
Repeat it, and use other means: flares, EPIRB
questions.why: An unanswered MAYDAY is repeated; meanwhile raise the alarm by every other means you have.

questions.q: After your MAYDAY you hear: "MAYDAY Blue Dolphin, this is Olympia Radio, RECEIVED MAYDAY". What does it tell you?
options: Your distress call has been received
Your call was unclear — send it again
Olympia Radio is calling another vessel
You must now downgrade to PAN-PAN
questions.why: RECEIVED MAYDAY is the acknowledgement: your distress has been heard and help is being organised.

questions.q: Nobody else seems to be responding to this call. What do you do on the radio now?

figure.title: Heard on 16
lines: Selene is 18 miles off — too far for you

options: Acknowledge Selene and keep to your course
Send a MAYDAY RELAY on 16 for Selene
Call Selene on channel 6 to check first
Keep silent — it is not your distress
questions.why: A MAYDAY that nobody acknowledges, when you cannot help yourself: relay it with MAYDAY RELAY.

questions.q: You are relaying another yacht's distress from your own yacht, Aura. How does your call begin?
options: MAYDAY ×3, THIS IS, the other yacht ×3
PAN-PAN ×3, THIS IS, Aura ×3
MAYDAY RELAY ×3, THIS IS, Aura ×3
MAYDAY RELAY ×3, THIS IS, the other yacht ×3
questions.why: A relay opens MAYDAY RELAY three times, then THIS IS and your own name — never pose as the casualty.

questions.q: You are sure this was a distress signal. Which radio call do you send?
options: Nothing until you know who fired it
PAN-PAN, as you do not know her name
MAYDAY in your own boat's name
MAYDAY RELAY, with what you saw and where
questions.why: A vessel in distress that cannot call for herself: you send a MAYDAY RELAY on her behalf.

questions.q: Before you step into the raft, what do you do about the VHF radios?
options: Take the handheld into the raft with you
Stay below on the fixed set to the end
Leave the handheld — it won't work in a raft
Leave the handheld aboard, still calling
questions.why: A handheld in the raft lets you talk to rescuers as they close in.

questions.q: The anchor will not hold again in time. Which call do you make, and when?

figure.title: Lee shore
lines: Six aboard, no room to sail off

options: Wait — try to re-anchor first, then call
MAYDAY now — the danger is grave and imminent
PAN-PAN now, MAYDAY once she hits the rocks
A routine call to the marina for a tow
questions.why: Do not wait for the impact: grave and imminent danger means MAYDAY now.

questions.q: Which call do you make?

figure.title: Crew overboard
lines: Lost sight of her in the waves

options: PAN-PAN — the yacht itself is not in danger
No call until you have searched for an hour
MAYDAY — a person in the water is in grave danger
SÉCURITÉ asking boats to keep a lookout
questions.why: A person overboard and lost from sight is in grave and imminent danger: MAYDAY.

questions.q: The skipper is unconscious, the boat is on fire, and you have no radio certificate. May you send the MAYDAY?
options: Only with the owner's consent by phone
Only from the handheld, not the fixed set
No — only a certificate holder may transmit
Yes — anyone aboard may send a distress call
questions.why: In distress anyone may use the radio; the certificate rule never stops a MAYDAY.

questions.q: The coast station is handling your MAYDAY for a fire, but you have now put the fire out and need no help. What do you do?
options: Tell the coast station at once that you need no help
Switch the radio off to keep 16 clear
Send a SÉCURITÉ saying that you are safe
Say nothing — the coastguard will work it out
questions.why: Rescuers keep coming until told: tell the station controlling the distress that you are safe.

questions.q: Which important items are missing from this message?

figure.title: Overheard MAYDAY
lines: MAYDAY Aura, 2 miles south of Poros

options: Destination and last port of call
Help needed and number of persons aboard
The time and the weather at the scene
The skipper's name and home port
questions.why: A distress message gives position, nature of distress, assistance required and persons on board.

questions.q: With no GPS fix, you use the lighthouse to find your place. How do you report your position in the MAYDAY?

figure.note: Bearing from your boat to the light

options: 330° from the lighthouse, 4 miles
4 miles from the lighthouse, no bearing
150° from the lighthouse, 4 miles
Your last GPS fix, an hour old
questions.why: Bearing is given FROM the landmark: the reciprocal of your bearing to it (330° − 180° = 150°).

questions.q: You have just finished giving your MAYDAY message. How do you end it, and then what?
options: Repeat it at once, without listening
Say OUT, then switch off to save power
Say OVER, then change to a working channel
Say OVER, then listen on 16 for an answer
questions.why: End with OVER and listen: the coast station or a nearby vessel will acknowledge on 16.

questions.q: You need help, but nobody aboard is in danger yet. Which call do you make on channel 16?
options: PAN-PAN
MAYDAY RELAY
SÉCURITÉ
MAYDAY
questions.why: Urgent help needed but no grave and imminent danger: PAN-PAN.

questions.q: You are about to send an urgency call to every station in range from your yacht Nefeli. How does it begin?
options: PAN-PAN ×3, THIS IS, Nefeli ×3, ALL STATIONS ×3
PAN-PAN ×3, ALL STATIONS ×3, THIS IS, Nefeli ×3
PAN-PAN once, ALL STATIONS once, THIS IS, Nefeli once
ALL STATIONS ×3, PAN-PAN ×3, THIS IS, Nefeli ×3
questions.why: Urgency call: PAN-PAN three times, the station(s) called, THIS IS, your name three times.

questions.q: Your crew member needs a doctor's view on what to do next. Which call do you make?
options: SÉCURITÉ, warning other yachts
MAYDAY, asking for a helicopter
PAN-PAN, asking for medical advice
A routine call to the Kos marina
questions.why: Medical help needed but no immediate threat to life: PAN-PAN with medical advice requested.

questions.q: You want a tow and only Olympia Radio needs to hear it. How do you address your PAN-PAN?
options: PAN-PAN ×3 with no address at all
Olympia Radio by voice on channel 70
PAN-PAN ×3, then ALL STATIONS ×3 only
PAN-PAN ×3, then Olympia Radio ×3
questions.why: An urgency call may go to all stations or to one named station, three times after PAN-PAN.

questions.q: Your problem has gone away on its own. What do you do about your earlier call?
options: Cancel the PAN-PAN: tell all stations you need no help
Send SEELONCE FEENEE on channel 16
Nothing — an urgency call expires by itself
Send a SÉCURITÉ that your engine runs
questions.why: Cancel an urgency call once the urgency is over, so nobody keeps looking for you.

questions.q: You pass this hazard in a busy channel. Which call warns the other vessels about it?
options: PAN-PAN
SÉCURITÉ
MAYDAY
MAYDAY RELAY
questions.why: A danger to navigation is a safety message: SÉCURITÉ.

questions.q: You hear a coast station on 16 begin: "SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, all stations…". What kind of message follows?
options: A call for help from a vessel in danger
A distress call — 16 goes silent
A navigational or weather warning
A list of calls waiting for ships
questions.why: SÉCURITÉ introduces a safety message: a navigational or weather warning.

questions.q: A coast station announces a SÉCURITÉ on 16 and says the gale warning follows on another channel, which it names. What do you do?
options: Stay on 16 — the warning comes there
Reply on 16 to acknowledge the warning
Ignore it unless your boat is named
Switch to the channel it named and listen
questions.why: The SÉCURITÉ is only announced on 16; the message itself goes out on the working channel given.

questions.q: You have finished the opening of your PAN-PAN to all stations. What comes next?
options: Your position, the problem and help needed
Nothing — wait for the coastguard to ask
The word MAYDAY, then your position
Only your MMSI, then wait to be called
questions.why: After the opening comes the message: position, nature of the urgency, assistance wanted.

questions.q: Things have changed since your urgency call went out. What do you do on the radio now?

figure.title: Still drifting
lines: You sent PAN-PAN for a tow

options: Send a SÉCURITÉ warning of the rocks
Upgrade to MAYDAY — the danger is now grave
Cancel the PAN-PAN and call a marina
Repeat the PAN-PAN every 15 minutes
questions.why: When the danger becomes grave and imminent, the urgency call is upgraded to MAYDAY.

questions.q: You have announced a SÉCURITÉ on 16 about a drifting container. Where do you give the warning itself?
options: On channel 70, as a DSC text message
Only to the coastguard, by phone
On a working channel you named on 16
On 16, straight after the announcement
questions.why: Keep 16 clear: announce there, then give the safety message on a working channel.

questions.q: The coast station acknowledges your medical PAN-PAN on 16 and asks you to change to a working channel. What do you do?
options: Refuse — medical calls need channel 16
Stay on 16 — urgency talk must stay there
Cancel the PAN-PAN before you change
Change channel and continue the talk there
questions.why: Long urgency traffic moves off 16 when the coast station asks, keeping 16 free.

questions.q: Which of these situations calls for a PAN-PAN?
options: Engine dead, drifting offshore, no danger yet
Booking a berth at the marina for tonight
Fire in the cabin that you cannot put out
A big log floating in the harbour approach
questions.why: PAN-PAN: urgent, but no grave and imminent danger. The fire is MAYDAY, the log SÉCURITÉ.

questions.q: You need a tow to the nearest port. Which call fits, and why?

figure.title: Dismasted
lines: Mast down, rig cut free and sunk

options: SÉCURITÉ — warn others of the lost rig
PAN-PAN — urgent, but no grave and imminent danger
MAYDAY — a dismasting is always a distress
No call — hail a passing yacht instead
questions.why: Help is needed urgently, but boat and crew are not in grave and imminent danger: PAN-PAN.

questions.q: Your guest is getting worse by the minute. Which call do you make?
options: PAN-PAN — medical cases are always urgency
PAN-PAN, asking for medical advice only
MAYDAY — a life is in grave and imminent danger
SÉCURITÉ, asking any doctor to call you
questions.why: A life-threatening condition is grave and imminent danger to a person: MAYDAY.

questions.q: A coast station is reading a SÉCURITÉ announcement on 16 just as you want to call a friend's yacht. What do you do?
options: Wait an hour before any routine call
Stay off 16 until SEELONCE FEENEE
Call over it — safety is low priority
Wait until it ends, then make your call
questions.why: Safety traffic comes before routine calls but imposes no silence: wait until it is over.

questions.q: The coast station answers your medical PAN-PAN and puts you through to a doctor. Which information helps the doctor most?
options: Age, symptoms and the first aid given
Passport number and nationality
The boat's insurance details
The name of their doctor at home
questions.why: Medical advice by radio needs the patient's age, symptoms and the treatment given so far.

questions.q: You see that a big mooring buoy has broken free and is drifting into the harbour approach. May your yacht send a SÉCURITÉ?
options: Only by DSC, never by voice
Yes — any station may warn of a danger
Only with the coastguard's permission
No — only coast stations send SÉCURITÉ
questions.why: Any station may send a safety message about a danger to navigation.

questions.q: Halfway through your own message, someone else breaks in on channel 16. What do you do?
options: Answer the PAN-PAN with your position
Finish your SÉCURITÉ — you started first
Stop, listen, and finish later if 16 is clear
Switch to high power and talk over it
questions.why: Urgency outranks safety: give way to the PAN-PAN, note it, and resume afterwards.

questions.q: The coast station has your PAN-PAN; a lifeboat will reach you in an hour. How do you use the radio while you wait?
options: Switch to 70 and wait for a DSC call
Call every five minutes for an update
Switch off to save the battery till it comes
Keep a listening watch on 16 and as told
questions.why: Stay reachable: keep watch on 16 or on the channel the coast station gave you.

questions.q: You hear a MAYDAY on 16 from a yacht you cannot see. What do you do first?
options: Listen, write it down, wait for the coast station
Answer at once to say you heard her
Call her back to ask for her position
Change channel to keep 16 clear
questions.why: First listen and record: a coast station normally acknowledges and coordinates.

questions.q: You can reach the sinking yacht in half an hour. What do you do on the radio?
options: Send a MAYDAY RELAY and keep your course
Acknowledge, then tell the coastguard you are going
Head there in silence to keep 16 clear
Keep listening — only coast stations acknowledge
questions.why: If no coast station answers and you can help, acknowledge the MAYDAY and inform the coastguard.

questions.q: You, on yacht Aura, acknowledge a MAYDAY from yacht Thalassa. Which form is right?
options: RECEIVED MAYDAY, with no names given at all
SEELONCE MAYDAY, Thalassa, THIS IS Aura
MAYDAY, Thalassa ×3, THIS IS, Aura ×3, RECEIVED MAYDAY
Thalassa, THIS IS Aura, ROGER your message, OVER
questions.why: Acknowledgement: MAYDAY, the casualty's name ×3, THIS IS, your name ×3, RECEIVED MAYDAY.

questions.q: During a rescue you hear the station controlling it say "SEELONCE MAYDAY". What does it require of you?
options: Repeat it so that more boats hear it
Switch your radio off until morning
Use low power for any routine calls
Keep off the channel unless you are in the rescue
questions.why: SEELONCE MAYDAY imposes silence: only stations taking part in the distress may transmit.

questions.q: You have kept quiet on 16 all afternoon during a rescue. Now you hear "SEELONCE FEENEE". What has changed?
options: Distress traffic is over; normal use resumes
The silence is extended for another hour
A second distress has begun nearby
Only short, essential calls are allowed
questions.why: SEELONCE FEENEE lifts radio silence: the distress traffic is over.

questions.q: During a rescue you have kept off 16. Now the station controlling the distress traffic announces "PRUDONCE". What does it tell you?
options: The distress is over and normal working resumes
The distress is not over, but restricted working may resume
Total silence on 16 until further notice
Only the vessel in distress may transmit
questions.why: PRUDONCE: restricted working may resume; full normal working comes only with SEELONCE FEENEE.

questions.q: You normally reach your friend on 16 first. With this going on, how do you get your message to her?

figure.title: On channel 16
lines: You want to tell a friend's yacht
that you will be late for dinner

options: Call quickly between the distress messages
Call her by voice on channel 70 instead
Leave 16 alone: wait, or reach her another way
Call on 16 on low power so nobody minds
questions.why: No routine traffic on a channel carrying distress working: wait, or find another way.

questions.q: A yacht's MAYDAY has been acknowledged and a search begins. Who coordinates it?
options: The yacht that sent the MAYDAY
The first yacht to reach the scene
The office of the nearest marina
The coastguard's rescue centre (MRCC)
questions.why: Search and rescue is coordinated by the MRCC, usually through a coast station.

questions.q: You are searching with other yachts, and the coastguard tells everyone on scene to work on channel 6. What do you do?
options: Use 6 for search talk, as directed
Stay on 16 — distress talk never leaves it
Use channel 70 so the talk goes by DSC
Pick your own quiet channel with the lifeboat
questions.why: On-scene talk uses the channel the coordinator directs, often 16 or 6.

questions.q: You hear a MAYDAY and reach for the log book. What do you write down?
options: Only the channel and the time you heard it
Name, position, problem, help needed, persons, time
Only the name of the vessel in distress
Nothing — the coast station records it all
questions.why: Note everything: you may have to relay it or help, and the coast station may not have heard.

questions.q: A helicopter lowers its winch wire towards your cockpit. What must happen before anyone touches it?
options: Someone ties it to a cleat to hold it steady
The crew turns the VHF off to avoid sparks
It touches the water or deck first, to earth it
The engine stops so the boat lies still
questions.why: The wire carries a static charge: let it earth on the sea or deck first, and never tie it to the boat.

questions.q: A rescue helicopter is hovering overhead and the noise is deafening. How do you get its instructions?
options: By hand signals only — VHF is not used
Shout up to the winchman as he comes down
Wait for a written note sent down the wire
Listen on VHF and do what the crew tells you
questions.why: Helicopter crews brief the yacht by VHF; follow their instructions exactly.

questions.q: The helicopter will arrive in ten minutes. How do you prepare the deck?

figure.title: Helicopter on its way
lines: To lift an injured crew member

options: Stow or lash down loose gear, clear a space
Hoist every sail so you are easy to see
Keep all crew on deck to catch the wire
Leave it — the downdraft will clear it
questions.why: Downdraft blows loose gear into the rotor and wire: secure everything and clear the pick-up area.

questions.q: You are much too far away to help this vessel. What do you do on the radio?
options: Acknowledge too, so she knows you heard
Keep listening and noting, but stay silent
Send a MAYDAY RELAY to make sure
Call her and offer your position
questions.why: Once a coast station has it, distant yachts keep quiet and listen — they may be asked to help later.

questions.q: You are close and could help the burning yacht. What do you do on the radio?

figure.title: MAYDAY nearby
lines: You can be there in 20 minutes

options: Nothing — the coast station has it in hand
Head there without a word to keep 16 clear
Offer help to the coast station, with your position
Acknowledge the burning yacht's MAYDAY yourself
questions.why: Offer your help to the station controlling the distress, with your position and ETA.

questions.q: Radio silence has been imposed, yet the rescue centre is calling you. May you answer?

figure.title: Silence imposed
lines: You are the yacht nearest the casualty
The MRCC calls you by name on 16

options: Only on channel 6, never on 16
No — SEELONCE MAYDAY silences everyone
Only after SEELONCE FEENEE is given
Yes — you are part of the distress traffic
questions.why: Radio silence binds stations not involved; those taking part in the rescue keep talking.

questions.q: During a long rescue you hear three signals over several hours. In which order do they normally come?
options: SEELONCE MAYDAY, PRUDONCE, SEELONCE FEENEE
PRUDONCE, SEELONCE MAYDAY, SEELONCE FEENEE
SEELONCE FEENEE, PRUDONCE, SEELONCE MAYDAY
SEELONCE MAYDAY, SEELONCE FEENEE, PRUDONCE
questions.why: Silence imposed, then restricted working allowed, then silence lifted.

questions.q: You might have found what everyone is looking for. What do you do on the radio?

figure.title: Searching
lines: Looking for a yacht's crew overboard
The MRCC gave you a search area
Something orange in the water ahead

options: Put out a SÉCURITÉ to all stations on 16
Report it to the coordinator on the channel in use
Wait until you are sure before saying anything
Send a new MAYDAY for the person in the water
questions.why: Report sightings at once to whoever coordinates the search, on the channel they set.

questions.q: You are heading to help a yacht in distress. The coastguard calls to say a lifeboat is there and you are not needed. What do you do?
options: Carry on anyway in case they need you
Ignore it — you already said you were going
Acknowledge the message and resume your passage
Ask for SEELONCE FEENEE before you turn
questions.why: Acknowledge your release by the coordinator; your help is no longer needed.

questions.q: The lifeboat cannot hear the yacht in distress, but you hear both. The MRCC asks you to pass messages between them. How?
options: Tell the yacht to shout louder into her set
Shorten them in your own words to save time
Refuse — only coast stations may relay
Pass each message on exactly as you heard it
questions.why: When relaying, pass messages on accurately and in full — the coordinator relies on them.

questions.q: Your 406 MHz EPIRB has been switched on. Which system carries its alert to a rescue centre?
options: Cospas-Sarsat satellites
NAVTEX coast stations
AIS shore stations
VHF DSC coast stations
questions.why: 406 MHz EPIRBs are detected by the Cospas-Sarsat satellite system, which passes alerts to MRCCs.

questions.q: A lifeboat is closing in on your liferaft, guided by your EPIRB. Which of its signals does she use for the final approach?
options: A 518 kHz NAVTEX signal
The 121.5 MHz homing signal
The 406 MHz satellite burst
A voice call on channel 16
questions.why: EPIRBs also send 121.5 MHz so rescuers can home in on them; 406 MHz goes to the satellites.

questions.q: You are buying an EPIRB for the boat. Why choose B?
options: It also makes voice calls on channel 16
It works without being registered
Its position reaches rescuers faster and more precisely
It needs no 121.5 MHz homing signal
questions.why: A GPS EPIRB sends its own position in the alert; without GPS the satellites must work it out.

questions.q: You buy a used yacht whose EPIRB is still registered to the previous owner. What do you do?
options: Switch it on once so the system learns you
Register it only if you sail offshore
Nothing — the registration stays with the beacon
Update the registration with your and the boat's details
questions.why: Rescuers use the registration to phone the owner and identify the boat: keep it current.

questions.q: What happens to this beacon if the yacht sinks before anyone can reach it?

figure.title: EPIRB on the pushpit
lines: In a bracket with a hydrostatic release

options: It floats free and switches itself on
It sends a DSC alert on channel 70
It stays in its bracket until someone frees it
It sinks with the boat, sealed in its bracket
questions.why: Category I: the hydrostatic release frees it at depth; it floats up and activates automatically.

questions.q: At the start of the season you want to check that the EPIRB works. How?
options: Drop it in a bucket of water to see it start
Run its self-test, as the maker's manual says
Leave it on overnight and see if anyone calls
Switch it on for a minute and call the coastguard
questions.why: Use only the built-in self-test, per the instructions; a real activation sends a live alert.

questions.q: You find the beacon has been transmitting by accident. What do you do?
options: Leave it on until the coastguard calls you
Send SEELONCE FEENEE on channel 16
Switch it off and tell the coastguard / MRCC
Switch it off and say nothing — it was brief
questions.why: A false alert may already be in the system: switch off and inform the coastguard at once.

questions.q: Your yacht has an EPIRB, and a crew member wears a PLB on her lifejacket. What is the key difference?
options: The PLB works only with a VHF DSC radio
The EPIRB is meant for inland waters only
The PLB uses only 121.5 MHz, no satellites
The EPIRB is registered to the boat, the PLB to a person
questions.why: Both alert via 406 MHz satellites; the EPIRB identifies the vessel, the PLB a person.

questions.q: You are in the liferaft and switch on the SART. What does it do?
options: Shows as a line of dots on a ship's radar
Sends your position to the satellites
Calls nearby ships by voice on 16
Flashes a light seen 10 miles away
questions.why: A SART answers a ship's 9 GHz (X-band) radar and paints a line of 12 dots on its screen.

questions.q: The rescue ship's radar shows this. Where exactly is the SART?

figure.title: Radar screen
lines: Running outwards, away from the ship

options: Anywhere along the line of dots
At the dot nearest the ship
In the middle of the line of dots
At the dot farthest from the ship
questions.why: The SART is at the first dot, the one closest to the ship; the line runs on beyond it.

questions.q: Your liferaft carries an AIS-SART instead of a radar SART. Who will see it?
options: Only the Cospas-Sarsat satellites
Only ships with a 9 GHz radar
Any vessel showing AIS targets
Only coast stations with NAVTEX
questions.why: An AIS-SART sends AIS messages with its position, shown on any AIS display nearby.

questions.q: You fit a NAVTEX receiver at the chart table. Which frequency does it listen on?
options: 406 MHz
518 kHz
questions.why: International NAVTEX broadcasts go out on 518 kHz, in English.

questions.q: Your NAVTEX prints this header. What does the letter B tell you about the message?
options: It is a meteorological warning
It is a navigational warning
It is search-and-rescue news
It is a routine weather forecast
questions.why: The second letter is the subject: A navigational warning, B meteorological warning, D SAR, E forecast.

questions.q: Your NAVTEX prints warnings from stations far from where you sail. How do you limit it to your area?
options: Set it to the local VHF channel
Select the letters of the local stations
Enter the local station's MMSI
Tune it to the local station's frequency
questions.why: All stations share 518 kHz; you choose which station letters (and message types) to print.

questions.q: A ferry nearby carries Class A AIS; your yacht has Class B. Which is true?
options: Class B only receives and never transmits
Class B gets priority over A in busy areas
Class B sends less often and at lower power
Class A is meant for yachts, B for ships
questions.why: Class A is the ship standard; Class B is a simpler small-craft set with lower power and slower reports.

questions.q: Does this mean the way ahead is clear of other vessels?
options: Yes — within 12 miles of the coast
Yes — only small fishing boats lack AIS
Yes — every vessel must transmit AIS
No — many boats have no AIS; keep a lookout
questions.why: AIS is an aid, not a lookout: many craft carry none or have it switched off.

questions.q: Your instructor says GMDSS changed rescue at sea. What is its main idea?
options: Distress alerts reach rescue centres automatically
Coast stations no longer listen on VHF
Every yacht must carry a satellite phone
Morse code is used for every distress alert
questions.why: GMDSS: automatic alerting (DSC, EPIRB) so a distress reaches shore even if no one hears a voice call.

questions.q: Which GMDSS sea area are you sailing in?

figure.title: Your cruising area
lines: In range of VHF DSC coast stations

options: A2
A1
A3
A4
questions.why: Sea area A1 is defined by the range of VHF DSC coast stations.

questions.q: Your passage takes you 80 miles offshore, beyond the range of VHF DSC coast stations. Which means can still alert a rescue centre from there?
options: AIS Class B, which alerts the MRCC
VHF DSC on high power — range doubles
A 406 MHz EPIRB, through the satellites
The NAVTEX receiver, which sends alerts
questions.why: Beyond A1 your VHF will not reach shore; a 406 MHz EPIRB alerts via satellite from anywhere.

questions.q: You are in the liferaft with a radar SART. Where do you put it?
options: Inside the canopy, on the floor
Under the raft, in a ballast pocket
In the water, tied to the raft
As high as possible, on its pole
questions.why: SART range depends on height: hold or mount it as high as you can.

questions.q: You charter a yacht with a fixed VHF. Which document covers the radio set itself?
options: The ship station radio licence
The boat's insurance policy
The charter contract
Your VHF operator's certificate
questions.why: The ship station licence covers the boat's radio equipment; the certificate covers the operator.

questions.q: You read through your boat's ship station licence. What does it list?
options: The skipper's name and qualification
The boat's call sign, MMSI and radio equipment
The crew list with passport numbers
The cruising area and the season dates
questions.why: The ship station licence names the vessel, its call sign, MMSI and licensed equipment.

questions.q: You sell your yacht and buy a different one. What happens to your VHF operator's certificate?
options: It passes to the buyer with the boat
It lapses when the old boat is sold
It stays with you — it is personal
It must be reissued for the new boat
questions.why: The operator's certificate belongs to the person; the station licence belongs to the boat.

questions.q: Your crew want to use the VHF to chat with friends on another yacht. Whose decision is it?
options: The coastguard's, by permission on air
Anyone's who holds a radio certificate
The owner's, even when not aboard
The skipper's — the radio is under their authority
questions.why: The ship's radio station is under the authority of the master or skipper.

questions.q: On a working channel you overhear two yachts discussing a private family matter. May you tell others what you heard?
options: No — overheard traffic must stay secret
Yes, but only to your own crew
Yes — it was on an open channel
Yes, once their conversation has ended
questions.why: Secrecy of correspondence: you may not pass on what you overhear (distress traffic aside).

questions.q: You noted down a MAYDAY that the coast station seems not to have heard. May you pass its details on to the coastguard?
options: Only with the casualty's permission
Yes — distress traffic is the exception
Only after SEELONCE FEENEE is given
No — secrecy covers all radio traffic
questions.why: Secrecy never stops you passing on distress traffic.

questions.q: Your guest is about to press the transmit key. What do you tell him?

figure.title: On deck
lines: A teenage guest picks up the mic
Wants to say MAYDAY "as a test"

options: Fine, as long as he uses low power
Fine, if he says "test" afterwards
No — a false distress call is prohibited
Fine on a working channel, not 16
questions.why: False or deceptive distress signals are forbidden and may launch a real rescue.

questions.q: Which of these transmissions breaks the radio rules?
options: A short radio check with the marina
A SÉCURITÉ about a drifting container
Calling the marina on its working channel
Calling the marina without giving your boat's name
questions.why: Every transmission must identify the station; transmissions without identification are prohibited.

questions.q: Bored on night watch, a crew member keeps clicking the transmit key on 16 to "say hello" to a friend's boat. What is wrong?
options: Unnecessary signals are prohibited
Nothing, since it is done at night
Nothing, if the set is on low power
Nothing, if the clicks are short
questions.why: Unnecessary transmissions and signals are prohibited — and they can mask a weak distress call.

questions.q: Several calls are waiting for a quiet channel. In which order of priority do they go?
options: Distress, safety, urgency, routine
Distress, urgency, safety, routine
Urgency, distress, safety, routine
Safety, distress, urgency, routine
questions.why: Priority: distress (MAYDAY), urgency (PAN-PAN), safety (SÉCURITÉ), then routine.

questions.q: Which radio traffic should you note in your log, like these entries?
options: Nothing — logs are only for big ships
Every routine call you make all day
Distress, urgency and safety traffic sent or heard
Only the calls that coast stations make
questions.why: Record distress, urgency and safety traffic heard or sent, with times — it may be needed later.

questions.q: You sail your own yacht, licensed in your home country, into Greek waters. Can you use her VHF there?
options: Only on channel 16, for nothing else
Only after registering at each port
No — she needs a Greek ship licence first
Yes, under her licence and the local rules
questions.why: A ship station licence is valid internationally; in foreign waters you also follow local regulations.

questions.q: Your crew member has no radio certificate. You hold one and stand beside her. May she call the marina?
options: Yes — under your supervision
No — only you may touch the set
Yes, but only on low power
Only calls to a coast station
questions.why: Someone without a certificate may operate the radio under the supervision of a certificate holder.

questions.q: May Anna make the routine call to the marina herself?

figure.title: Afternoon at anchor
lines: Anna wants to book a berth by VHF

options: Yes — routine calls need no certificate
Not alone — she must wait for you
Yes, if she gives your certificate number
Yes, if she keeps the set on low power
questions.why: Without a certificate she may only operate under a holder's supervision (distress excepted).

questions.q: Your crew member is losing his temper on the radio. What do you do?

figure.title: Berth dispute
lines: Another skipper took your booked berth
Your crew grabs the VHF, furious
Starts swearing at him on air

options: Let him finish, then apologise yourself
Let him, as long as he gives the boat name
Stop him — obscene language is prohibited
Let him — it is only a working channel
questions.why: Obscene or abusive language on the radio is prohibited.

questions.q: Three messages are waiting to go out. In which order should they be sent?

figure.title: Waiting to transmit
lines: A: engine dead, drifting, tow needed
B: warning of an unlit buoy

options: A, C, B
B, A, C
C, A, B
A, B, C
questions.why: Urgency (drifting without engine, PAN-PAN) before safety (the buoy, SÉCURITÉ) before routine.

questions.q: Ashore at a taverna, you want to call your crew on the boat with the yacht's handheld marine VHF. Is that allowed?
options: No — marine VHF is not for use from land
Yes, on low power only
Yes, within a mile of the boat
Yes, on channel 16 only
questions.why: Marine VHF is licensed for the maritime service; using it from land generally needs special permission.

questions.q: With these papers aboard, may you use the charter yacht's VHF?

figure.title: Charter yacht
lines: Ship licence: in the charter firm's name

options: No — the licence must be in your own name
Yes — her licence and your certificate cover it
Only once the firm informs the coastguard
Only on channel 16, and only in distress
questions.why: The boat's station licence covers the set; your certificate covers you as the operator.

questions.q: A port official inspecting your yacht asks for her radio documents. What do you show?
options: Only your passport and the crew list
The VHF's manual and its receipt
Ship station licence and operator's certificate
The charter contract and insurance
questions.why: Keep the station licence and the operator's certificate aboard, ready for inspection.

questions.q: A friend suggests you use his boat's name on your radio so that your own boat stays "off the air". What do you say?
options: Fine, if his boat is not at sea today
Fine, as long as you use low power
Fine, but only on working channels
No — false identification is prohibited
questions.why: You must identify your own station correctly; false identification is prohibited.
